title: Costs
overview: Cost information supports pricing, output and investment decisions. AS questions commonly require accurate contribution, break-even and margin-of-safety calculations followed by interpretation of what changes the risk and whether the simplifying assumptions are realistic.
syllabusPoints: Distinguish fixed, variable, total, average, direct and indirect costs.
Calculate total cost, average cost, total revenue, profit and contribution.
Calculate break-even output and margin of safety.
Analyse how changes in price, fixed cost, variable cost and output affect break-even and profit.
Assess the uses and limitations of cost and break-even information.

definitions.definition: A cost that does not change with output in the short run, including when output is zero.
A cost that changes directly with the level of output or sales.
Total fixed cost plus total variable cost.
Total cost per unit of output.
A cost that can be traced directly to a product, service, job or cost unit.
A shared overhead that cannot be economically traced to one product or cost unit.
Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit; the amount each unit contributes to fixed cost and then profit.
Contribution per unit multiplied by units sold, or total revenue minus total variable cost.
The output at which total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero.
Actual or forecast sales volume minus break-even output.
A cost containing both a fixed element and a variable element.

sections.title: Classifying costs
content: Fixed cost is unchanged across a relevant short-run output range, such as rent or salaried management. Variable cost rises with output, such as direct material or piece-rate labour. Direct/indirect is a different classification based on traceability, so a cost can be fixed and direct or variable and indirect depending on context.
bullets: Some costs are stepped or semi-variable: an extra supervisor or machine may be needed after a capacity threshold.
Classify using the case and time period rather than memorising one label for every wage or utility cost.
Accurate classification matters because contribution and break-even use variable cost, not all cost per unit.

sections.title: Using total, average and marginal information
content: Total cost supports profit and cash planning; average cost informs long-run pricing and efficiency comparison; marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit. Decisions may fail if managers use historic averages for a short-run order whose relevant extra cost is different.
bullets: Price normally needs to cover total cost in the long run.
A special order above variable cost can add contribution when spare capacity exists, but it may affect regular customers or trigger extra fixed cost.
Cost data should be current, relevant and interpreted with qualitative evidence.

sections.title: Contribution
content: Each unit's contribution first covers fixed cost. Once total contribution equals fixed cost, the business breaks even; further contribution becomes profit. A product with positive contribution can support the business even if allocated average cost appears high.
bullets: Contribution is not profit until fixed cost has been covered.
Higher price or lower variable cost increases contribution, reducing break-even output if fixed cost is unchanged.
Capacity, demand and competitor response determine whether the planned number of units can actually be sold.

examples.label: Contribution and profit
examples.content: Price $30; variable cost $18; fixed cost $24,000; sales 2,500 units. Contribution per unit = $12. Total contribution = $30,000. Profit = $30,000 − $24,000 = $6,000.

sections.title: Break-even calculations
content: Break-even output divides fixed cost by contribution per unit. Margin of safety shows how far expected/actual sales can fall before loss begins. A higher margin usually means lower operating risk, but it says nothing by itself about cash timing, quality or future demand.
bullets: Round break-even output up to the next whole unit when a fraction is produced.
State units, not dollars, unless the question requests break-even revenue.
Profit at a chosen output can be calculated as total contribution minus fixed cost.

examples.label: Break-even and safety
examples.content: Fixed cost $45,000; price $25; variable cost $10. Contribution = $15. Break-even = 45,000 ÷ 15 = 3,000 units. At sales of 4,200, margin of safety = 1,200 units.

sections.title: Constructing and reading a break-even chart
content: Put output on the horizontal axis and cost/revenue on the vertical. Fixed cost is horizontal within the range. Total cost starts at fixed cost and rises by variable cost per unit. Total revenue starts at zero and rises by selling price. The intersection is break-even; loss lies where total cost exceeds revenue and profit where revenue exceeds cost.
bullets: The vertical gap between total revenue and total cost at an output is profit or loss.
Margin of safety is the horizontal gap between actual/forecast output and break-even output.
Label axes, lines, break-even and the relevant output clearly.

sections.title: How changes move break-even
content: Higher fixed cost raises the total-cost intercept and break-even output. Higher variable cost steepens total cost, reduces contribution and raises break-even. Higher price steepens revenue, increases contribution and lowers break-even—if sales volume does not fall. A lower price has the reverse arithmetic effect but may increase demand.
bullets: Mechanisation often raises fixed cost while lowering variable cost: it may raise break-even but improve profit at high output.
Use revised calculations for a 'what if' decision and then discuss whether the assumed sales are realistic.

sections.title: Uses of cost and break-even data
content: Managers can set target sales, compare locations or production methods, assess a price/cost change, judge a new product and present evidence to lenders. The model makes relationships visible and supports sensitivity analysis.
bullets: It helps answer 'what must be sold?', not 'what will be sold?'.
Combine with market research, capacity, cash-flow, quality and stakeholder evidence.

sections.title: Limitations of break-even analysis
content: The model usually assumes constant price and variable cost, fixed cost unchanged within the range, all output sold, one product or constant sales mix, and accurate linear estimates. In reality discounts, overtime, stock, capacity steps and uncertainty change the lines.
bullets: Multi-product businesses require an assumed sales mix; if that mix changes, the calculated break-even changes.
Inflation and external shocks can make the data quickly outdated.
The simplicity is valuable for comparison, but should not be mistaken for a forecast of actual demand.

formulas.label: Total cost
formulas.expression: Total fixed cost + total variable cost

formulas.label: Contribution per unit
formulas.expression: Selling price per unit − variable cost per unit

formulas.label: Margin of safety
formulas.expression: Actual or forecast output − break-even output

comparisonTable.title: Effect on break-even output
rows: Price or supplier response may follow

diagram.title: Contribution-to-profit logic
nodes: Remainder is profit or shortfall is loss

analysisChains.title: Reducing variable cost
steps: Fewer units are needed to cover fixed cost
Break-even output falls and margin of safety may rise
Profit at the same sales volume increases
analysisChains.evaluation: Cheaper inputs may reduce quality and demand; negotiate or reduce waste before assuming the saving is sustainable.

analysisChains.title: Automation and break-even
steps: Labour/defect variable cost per unit may fall
Contribution increases but the fixed-cost base is larger
Profit improves only above the crossover output
analysisChains.evaluation: The better method depends on expected demand, capacity utilisation, finance and technology risk—not break-even alone.

analysisChains.title: Increasing price
steps: Actual profit could decline if lost volume is large
analysisChains.evaluation: Use PED, competitor response and brand strength before recommending the higher price.

examTips: Write the formula, substitute numbers, show working and include units.
Use contribution per unit—not average cost—in the break-even formula.
After every calculation, interpret what the result means for the business decision and risk.
For a chart, label fixed cost, total cost, total revenue, break-even and both axes.
commonMistakes: Calling contribution per unit profit per unit before fixed cost is covered.
Subtracting break-even output from actual output in the wrong direction for margin of safety.
Assuming all fixed costs remain fixed at any scale.
Using the calculated break-even as a sales forecast.
Ignoring demand when suggesting a price rise to lower break-even.

quickRecall.question: How is contribution per unit calculated?
quickRecall.answer: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit.

quickRecall.question: What happens to contribution before break-even?
quickRecall.answer: It accumulates to cover fixed cost.

quickRecall.question: How is break-even output calculated?
quickRecall.answer: Fixed costs divided by contribution per unit.

quickRecall.question: How is margin of safety calculated?
quickRecall.answer: Actual or forecast output minus break-even output.

quickRecall.question: Where does total cost start on a break-even chart?
quickRecall.answer: At the fixed-cost value on the vertical axis when output is zero.

quickRecall.question: Why might a price rise lower calculated break-even but reduce actual profit?
quickRecall.answer: The higher price raises contribution, but demand may fall enough to reduce total contribution.

quickRecall.question: Name two major break-even assumptions.
quickRecall.answer: Examples: constant price/variable cost, fixed cost unchanged, all output sold, constant sales mix and linear relationships.
